dialogue.text: [serious, engaging] And on day three, the one thing everyone says will protect you starts falling.

[serious, engaging] Mumbai. India loves gold, and in a crash, families who need cash bring their gold to the jeweler. They expect a great price, because gold is supposed to go up when everything else goes down.
Madam, I didn't change the price. The world changed the price. Twice, since you walked in.

[serious, engaging] Gold is falling because the big investors who borrowed to bet on stocks have to pay those loans back today, and gold is the fastest thing on Earth to turn into cash. It happened just last month: tech stocks fell, and gold dropped below four thousand dollars an ounce, almost thirty percent under its January record. So if your emergency plan was gold, it got cheaper the very week you needed it.
[serious, engaging] End of week one, and the crash spreads around the world through the one thing everyone suddenly wants: dollars.

[serious, engaging] In a panic, money everywhere runs into the dollar, so the dollar gets stronger, even though the mess started in America. And because oil and wheat are paid for in dollars, if you live outside America, your gas and your groceries now cost more, even if nothing changed where you live.
[serious, engaging] Cairo feels it first. Egypt is one of the biggest wheat buyers in the world.
